layer1_summary.paragraph: The physical symbols and ceremonial objects of Iron Arrow — its jackets, arrows, pins, and regalia — represent the society's deep roots in Seminole tradition and its evolving identity across decades at the University of Miami. This section also captures milestone moments, from the 50th anniversary golden celebration to the football glory years, that illustrate how Iron Arrow's material culture and communal rituals reinforced its prestige and sense of continuity.
bullets: The fiftieth anniversary celebration on October 31, 1976, at the Riviera Country Club brought together surviving founders including Johnnie McGuire, Bob Fink, Norman Ted Kennedy, and Francis S. Houghtaling for what member Clive Shrader called "the finest social event in the history of Iron Arrow."
Francis S. Houghtaling was awarded the Bowman Foster Ashe In-Memoriam Honor at the golden anniversary by Chief John Benedict, recognizing extraordinary service to the society's founding legacy.

Iron Arrow's paraphernalia — including the Iron Arrow flag, membership plaques, scrapbooks, and a three-foot photo of the founding nine — served as tangible links to the society's origins and were prominently displayed at major gatherings.

A typical year of Iron Arrow activity, as summarized in Chief John Benedict's 1975 bulletin, included community service efforts such as sponsoring underprivileged children at football games, funding Band of the Hour uniforms, and injecting campus palm trees to combat blight.

The first Iron Arrow Seminole Scholarship was awarded in October 1974 to Ron Scott, a senior drama major of Osage Indian heritage, representing one of the rare instances of a collegiate organization offering a scholarship specifically to an American Indian student.

THE ARROW

ASHE IN-MEMORIAM HONOR
- The Bowman Foster Ashe In-Memoriam Honor was awarded on October 31, 1976, at Iron Arrow's fiftieth anniversary celebration
- Award presented by Chief John Benedict to Francis S. Houghtaling at the Riviera Country Club of Coral Gables
- The award and Houghtaling's receipt of it are documented in the Tribe's videotape, "UM's Living History: Iron Arrow"

IRON ARROW PINS
- No subsection content on Iron Arrow Pins appears in the provided source text pages (126–131)

BITS AND PIECES
- April 24, 1975: Chief John Benedict mailed an Iron Arrow bulletin summarizing the tribe's preceding year's activities; the list was four pages long
- Homecoming Reception held at President Stanford's new home on Old Cutler Road drew over 300 members and guests
- Fourth annual Underprivileged Children's football game was the UM-Pacific game; over 90 children were treated to hot dogs, Coke, and ice cream; Hurricanes won 35–7
- Iron Arrow members manned all phones one night at the annual Alumni Loyalty Fund phone campaign; members obtained pledges of $7,080, a 50 percent increase over the previous year's high
- Nearly 150 members and tappees participated in pregame and half-time lineups greeting the team at the Homecoming game
- Iron Arrow sponsored injection of 77 palm trees on campus to combat palm blight; further treatments noted as required
- Tribe raised $960.00 toward new uniforms for the Band of the Hour
- Iron Arrow aided in the sale of football season tickets; 54 season tickets valued at $44.00 each were sold during a week-long campaign
- First Iron Arrow Seminole Scholarship awarded in October (1974–1975 academic year) to Ron Scott, a senior drama major whose Osage Indian name is Running Deer, who faced leaving school due to lack of tuition funds; scholarship enabled him to graduate in December 1974
- Seminole Scholarship Fund described as "one of the few instances in the nation where a collegiate organization offers a scholarship to the American Indian"
- Fund contained $2,000 at time of report, due to efforts of members Julian Cole and Luther Evans
- University granted a tuition waiver for an Indian student upon request of the tribe; Dr. Stanford announced the waiver at the Homecoming luncheon
- Neither the Seminole artifact collection nor the Lignum Vitae archaeological project was completed; funds already collected were diverted to similar purposes, including a donation to the James Hutchinson Fund
- The State of Florida, urged by The Nature Conservancy, purchased Lignum Vitae Key to preserve its natural environment, described as containing "one of the largest stands of West Indian virgin tropical flora left in the continental United States"; the state subsequently postponed or permanently shelved the proposed archaeological excavation of the mound

THE NEW BEGINNING
- No subsection content on The New Beginning appears in the provided source text pages (126–131)

IRON ARROW AT A GLANCE
- Six principles identified in the Epilogue as underlying Iron Arrow's success:
- 1. Power of the Indian tradition: Iron Arrow draws traditions from American Indian cultures rather than Greek mythology; described as rooted in nature, wilderness, and its values
- 2. Balance between intense visibility and impenetrable secrecy: ceremonial jackets, drum, Arrow, plaque, firebowl, statue of Ashe, and tapping ritual cited as separate innovations that evolved into "one dramatic unity"; mystery around meetings and initiation ceremonies described as "a powerful ally of the IA phenomenon"
- 3. Unanimity of selection: membership requires unanimous vote; described as the tradition of the American Indian (citing Alvin M. Josephy, "The Indian Heritage of America"); warned that "absence of argument or contention during the selection process should alarm us"; standard of "number of man hours" times "impact" proposed as a bridge across changing times
- 4. Lifetime voting rights: "Every member always has a vote: for life"
- 5. The initiation ritual: described as "one arduous, symbolic event shared between Iron Arrows and no others"; quality varies year to year; Medicine Man must practice for dramatic impact; ritual suffers from too few or too many participants administering it
- 6. Continuity through long-association members: Iron Arrow always needs "at least one or two members, officers or advisors, whose association with the tribe will provide it with protection and continuity"

THE FOOTBALL GLORY YEARS
- Golden anniversary celebration held October 31, 1976, at the Riviera Country Club of Coral Gables
- Described as "the last time that most of the surviving founders of Iron Arrow would gather with younger members from the Tribe's first fifty years"
- Founders present: Johnnie McGuire, Bob Fink, Norman Ted Kennedy, Francis S. Houghtaling
- Howard Osceola attended the celebration
- Iron Arrow member Mike Braz played piano during reception, including "The Sheik of Araby," "Perfidia," and Irving Berlin's "What'll I Do?"
- Film from the evening showed a table of Iron Arrow historical memorabilia, the Iron Arrow flag, membership plaques, scrapbooks, and a three-foot-long photo of the founding nine
- Members in attendance: Armando "Stitch" Vari, Bryce Dunham, Sid Weisburd, Mike Braz, Thad Koch, Joe Mancuso, Drew Vella, Steve Hill, Henry Minich, Henry King Stanford, Joe Shaw, Randolph Femmer, Bob Rosen, Michael Leone, Dave Brown, Walt Kichefski, Clive Shrader
- Clive Shrader described the evening banquet as "the finest social event in the history of Iron Arrow"
- Tribe's videotape "UM's Living History: Iron Arrow" highlights film from the evening, including Houghtaling's receipt of the Ashe In-Memoriam, a portrait presentation to President Henry King Stanford, and a closing scene of Johnnie McGuire signaling "Number One"
- Homecoming week 1976 also featured a luncheon and reception for all past Iron Arrow officers at Howard Osceola's village at Twenty Mile Bend in the Everglades
- Film footage of UM's homecoming parade down Miracle Mile in Coral Gables shows Francis Houghtaling, Rhea Warren, and John Benedict riding in a carriage; Michael Leone and Drew Vella riding on sideboards of 1920-era Model T Fords
